cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a decorated Armenian earthenware jug with incised and painted ornament, consistent with the claimed Armenian origin and metadata.

physical.title: Jug
physical.medium_raw: Earthenware with underglaze decoration, painted over white slip and incised
physical.physical_description: Jug of red earthenware, with an ovoid body slightly flattened on the sides, short narrow neck, expanding mouth, short curved spout connected with the mouth by a band with a serrated ridge. The body is decorated with applied ridges forming compartments of irregular shape in which are incised rosettes and geometrical and other devices.  The body is covered in white slip with through which decoration has been incised, sgraffiato, and streaked with green under a yellow glaze. Below the handle is an inscription in Armenian.
physical.historical_context:
The Empire of Trebizond was established after the fall of Constantinople in 1204. It was located on the Black Sea. In 1461 it fell to the Ottomans. The city of Trebizond is now called Trabzon
Note in Ceramics Department's register, 
"Compare with a jug in the Kaiser Friedrich Museum, Berlin, illustrated in 'Amth. Berichte aus den kgl. Kunst sammlungen', 38, 1916-17, Abb. 54 (article O. Wulff, 'Neu erwerbungen Mittelalterlichen Byzantinisches Keramik' p. 179), where 15th century is suggested as a date."
Their jug was acquired in 1915 apparently in Constantinople. It is described as imitating an Islamic metalware shape with the exception of the spout. The applied slipware 'cords' resemble ropework wrapped around an object to facilitate carrying.
The jug is covered with white slip and a very dark brown glaze. The decoration consists of stylised roses and three peacocks.
Are only assuming it to have been made in Constantinople and during the latter days of Greek rule or the early days of Ottoman rule.
